title: Grey hair would warn him, if he would heed it
intro: Al-Buhturi praises Ali ibn Murr of Tayy in a poem that his editor Hasan Kamil al-Sayrafi tentatively dates to 222 AH (836–837 CE). It opens with a woman’s rebuke over grey hair, desire and empty pockets, then reckons up twenty unprofitable months in Samarra. The poet who has struggled to find listeners ends by giving poetry itself a voice in choosing whom to praise.

translation: There is a warning for him in grey hair, if he would heed it,
a preacher there, if he were anything but stone.
1.sharh: The preacher is already there on the man’s own head. A warning so close could fail only with someone as insensible as stone.

translation: What once was black at his temples has turned white.
Broad daylight reclaimed what dawn had overlooked.
2.sharh: As the first faint light leaves patches dark, the first grey hairs left some black at the temples. Full daylight comes back to claim the remainder.

translation: A young man has ample time for love
until the hair at the edges of his head dies.
3.sharh: Black hair is given a lifespan of its own. The general rule about a young man’s time for love sets up the very personal reproach that follows.

translation: She said, “Grey hair and love. You go between them.
Love at that age is a sin past forgiving.”
4.sharh: The woman treats the conjunction of age and desire as an offence. Her little “that in that” points back to the two words with which she opened her case.

translation: In ignorance she taunted me with bucketfuls of want.
The bow tree stands bare, no fruit upon its bough.
5.sharh: She sees only what poverty has stripped from him. A fruitless tree may have just the wood a bowmaker prizes, a value her way of reckoning misses.

translation: The man you have so often taunted is scarcely poor.
It is the age that stands in need of free spirits.
6.sharh: Her taunts measure poverty in money. In his account the age itself is the dependant, since it cannot supply for itself the dignity such people bring.

translation: It consoles me for lost fortune that the incapable attain it.
Knowing who has riches makes my hardship lighter.
7.sharh: The people who prosper have done him an unexpected service. Their example removes any reason to take his own hard luck as a verdict on his abilities.

translation: Of most people now nothing remains
for the mind to grasp except these outward shapes.
8.sharh: Outward form survives after the qualities that would make a person worth knowing have gone. Even the imagination can find nothing further to work with.

translation: Meanness and ignorance. Either one is enough
to wipe out the trace a man leaves behind.
9.sharh: One fault closes the hand, the other the mind. Either can erase the track by which a later generation might have known the man.

translation: If the very merits on which I pride myself
are my offences, tell me how I can apologise.
10.sharh: His best evidence for the defence has already been admitted as evidence against him. An apology would mean repudiating the very qualities on which his case rests.

translation: I try to rouse with verse men so drowsy
in their ignorance they would scarcely feel a sword.
11.sharh: A poet tries to wake men whom even a sword blow would leave insensible. In Arabic the word for poetry and the verb “feel” have the same root.

translation: My task is to carve the rhymes where the stone breaks.
What is it to me if the cattle cannot understand?
12.sharh: Carving a rhyme takes skill and a sense of where the material will yield. His responsibility ends once that work is done, and his listeners take the full force of the insult.

translation: I swear I shall leave, my hopes cast aside
in Samarra, with fate so slow to answer them.
13.sharh: His hopes seem left behind like discarded belongings. The old name of Samarra, meaning “a joy to whoever sees it”, is particularly sharp in such a farewell.

translation: After twenty months, no gift in sight
to take home, no promise worth staying for.
14.sharh: Twenty months have produced neither of the things that could settle his plans, something in hand for the journey home or a reason to remain.

translation: Had it not been for Ali ibn Murr,
we would still suck at life’s teat, full of bitter sap and aloes.
15.sharh: Ali changes what life has to offer the speaker. Its teat gives bitter plant juices where milk should flow, and the father’s name, Murr, echoes the Arabic for bitter.

translation: We sought shelter with a lord whose furthest gift is near
to those who ask, whose least endeavour is a journey.
16.sharh: The distances depend on who is travelling. The petitioner has only a short way to reach Ali’s most distant bounty, while other men would have to journey to match his smallest effort.

translation: He gives and gives, and his clouds do no harm.
Rain sometimes does harm when it persists.
17.sharh: Rain is the customary likeness for generosity, until too much of it floods a field. Ali can persist in giving without acquiring that defect of his model.

translation: Giving away his gifts never tires his spirit.
Who ever saw an eye worn out by seeing?
18.sharh: Giving is an exercise of his nature as seeing is of the eye. The emphasis falls on the ease of the action, even when it is repeated.

translation: A full measure of his favour reached the desert folk.
The townsfolk witness another just as plentiful.
19.sharh: The open country and the settled town receive matching endowments. The line gives each population room to experience his generosity for itself.

translation: Gifts for which we never had to face the trouble of asking.
A cloud is a well that no one has to dig.
20.sharh: Water normally costs a well-digger labour. Call a rain cloud a well and the labour disappears, as petitioning disappears from this account of Ali’s gifts.

translation: We hold him in awe, though his gaze sends no sparks
across the gathering and his cheek is never turned in pride.
21.sharh: The assembly accords him respect without a threatening eye or an ostentatiously averted face. His authority can be felt even when its familiar gestures are absent.

translation: Cool at heart when fear blazes like the noonday heat,
he stokes the fire when war’s bright brand catches.
22.sharh: The heat has two sources, terror and battle. One cannot disturb him inside, while the other draws an active response from the same cool man.

translation: When he climbs to the heights of judgement, he can see
even what the unseen world keeps hidden.
23.sharh: Foresight takes the form of a view from higher ground. Consequences out of sight at ordinary eye level come into range as his judgement climbs.

translation: He stands midway through the ages of a life, neither too young
for the troubles that come upon him nor too old.
24.sharh: Ali is mature enough to have met trouble and vigorous enough to take it on. Midlife supplies the balance the next verse will measure in the shaft of a spear.

translation: Like a spear measuring ten cubits and one,
neither too long nor too short for its purpose.
25.sharh: The eleven-cubit spear gives a precise figure for proportion. Its merit lies in fitting its use, and another cubit would not make it better.

translation: A seasoned man, whose resolves often dismayed
men of judgement while he was the untried youth among them.
26.sharh: Maturity has confirmed an ability already glimpsed in the untried boy. The contrast sharpens when we learn that the men he disconcerted were themselves reputed wise.

translation: Today his judgements are swords of Indian steel.
He was sword-sharp when his ideas were still iron billets.
27.sharh: Judgement has gone through a smith’s workshop. The younger man already cut like a sword when the material of his mature decisions was still unworked metal.

translation: He climbs the high ridges of glory
with a heart so steady he might be walking downhill.
28.sharh: The height tells us what the ascent actually costs. His composure makes the climb look as effortless as a descent.

translation: He kept coming first until the very man who envied him said,
“He must know a short way to the heights.”
29.sharh: The jealous rival invents a shortcut to explain all those victories. Even his attempt to discount them ends by admitting how far ahead Ali has gone.

translation: Pure sweetness, when you gather his goodwill as your fruit,
yet sharply bitter when you rouse him to anger.
30.sharh: Disposition is fruit to be gathered and tasted. How the visitor treats Ali determines which of two utterly different flavours it yields.

translation: I warned his enviers off and told them,
“A flood by night spares nothing and leaves nothing.”
31.sharh: A flash flood is most terrifying when darkness conceals its advance. The warning replaces Ali’s name with the one thing his enemies ought to imagine approaching.

translation: Hold back, or you will be held back with regret smouldering
when the leopard turns fierce in its charge.
32.sharh: One change of voice turns “stop” into “be stopped”. The flood gives way to an animal in the instant before its full force is felt.

translation: An obstinate fighter, he wears his enemies out in close combat,
and goes home with victory in his claws.
33.sharh: The Arabic words for victory and claws almost coincide. The wordplay lets the wild animal of the preceding verse keep its grip on the image.

translation: It is mean to venture within the reach of his anger
because you know he will pardon once he has the power.
34.sharh: The offender has calculated on Ali’s clemency. The same pardon that honours the powerful man exposes the baseness of someone who uses it as insurance.

translation: He shuns his bed, ever amid a clamour
whose brilliance almost lends the moon its light.
35.sharh: The noise of the host keeps him away from his bed. Its simultaneous blaze of light reverses the usual night scene, making the moon almost a borrower.

translation: When Khutama marches in his host, taking
Nabhan’s leading rope, all thorns and trees,
36.sharh: Khutama and Nabhan are names within Tayy. The near repetition of Khutama and khitam, a leading rope, locks the moving ranks together in sound.

translation: you see glory with your own eyes among the sons of Udad,
while other tribes’ glory reaches you by report.
37.sharh: The sentence begun with the march now reaches its conclusion. A living tribal muster makes a different claim on belief from a pedigree recounted second-hand.

translation: Treat poetry well, Abu Hasan. Its stars have begun
to scatter their praise upon you.
38.sharh: The turn to Ali’s familiar title brings the exchange back into the room. Poetic lines become stars showering the person who has given them a subject.

translation: The rhymes came to you on the heels of a gift,
as blossoms open after driving rain.
39.sharh: Here the sequence matters. The benefaction is the downpour, and the rhymes are the visible growth that follows it.

translation: There are carnelians and native gold in them, if worn
on a day of display, and figured cloth and striped robes.
40.sharh: The poem becomes an outfit for a public occasion. Jewels flash separately, while patterned and striped fabrics get their beauty from how the threads sit together.

translation: Another man may boast of verse that praises him
in its folds. Poetry itself boasts of you.
41.sharh: The figure of the preceding verse makes a poem something with folds. Inside them the usual transaction is reversed, and the verse can claim the man as its distinction.

1.1.3.head: زَجر
1.1.3.meaning: A warning meant to check a course of action.

1.2.1.head: واعِظ
1.2.1.meaning: A preacher or admonisher. Al-Barquqi prints “one who gets through to him”.

2.1.5.head: فَود
2.1.5.meaning: A temple, the side of the head bordering the ear.

2.2.1.head: جَلِيَّة
2.2.1.meaning: The clear, fully revealed light of morning.

3.1.2.head: مُهلَة
3.1.2.meaning: A period of grace before a limit is reached.

4.1.4.head: راحَ
4.1.4.meaning: To go about in a given state. Al-Barquqi’s text has “you are between them”.

5.1.2.head: سِجال
5.1.2.meaning: Large buckets, used here to measure repeated drenchings of poverty.

5.2.1.head: النَّبع
5.2.1.meaning: Nab', a tree valued for its tough bow wood.

7.1.3.head: حَظّ
7.1.3.meaning: One’s share of good fortune, particularly worldly advancement.

7.2.6.head: يُسُر
7.2.6.meaning: Wealth or ease, as opposed to hardship. The extra short vowel in yusur fills out the rhyme.

9.2.2.meaning: Those two, meaning meanness and ignorance.

9.2.4.head: عَفّى
9.2.4.meaning: To efface a track or obliterate a trace.

10.1.3.meaning: “Which”, referring to his qualities. Both editions give the plural «اللاتي», with a long vowel after the doubled l. The singer stretches the syllable, so the two forms are hard to distinguish.

10.1.4.head: أَدَلَّ
10.1.4.meaning: To take confident pride in something or rely on it as a claim.

11.1.5.head: وَسَن
11.1.5.meaning: Drowsiness on the edge of sleep.

12.1.2.head: نَحت
12.1.2.meaning: Carving a form from stone or wood, here the making of verse.

12.1.5.head: مَقطَع
12.1.5.meaning: A cutting place, the point where material can be worked.

12.2.3-4.meaning: “If [they] do not.” Both diwan texts have “for them to”, and al-Sayrafi records the performed wording in his apparatus.

13.2.1-3.head: سُرَّ مَن رَأى
13.2.1-3.meaning: Samarra, the Abbasid capital on the Tigris. Its name was expanded as Surra man ra'a.

15.1.2-4.head: عَلِيّ بن مُرّ
15.1.2-4.meaning: Ali ibn Murr, a member of Tayy addressed later as Abu Hasan.

15.2.5-6.head: الصّاب وَالصَّبِر
15.2.5-6.meaning: Bitter plant juices, the second the juice of aloes.

16.2.2.head: العُفاة
16.2.2.meaning: Petitioners who come seeking a gift.

17.1.1.meaning: To persist, here in the giving of gifts.

19.1.6.head: سابِغَة
19.1.6.meaning: Ample and enfolding, like a garment that covers its wearer.

21.2.6.head: صَعَر
21.2.6.meaning: Turning one’s cheek away in disdain.

22.2.1.head: مِسعَر
22.2.1.meaning: A stoker of fire, hence one who kindles battle.

25.1.2.head: ذِراع
25.1.2.meaning: A cubit, approximately the distance from elbow to fingertip.

27.2.5.head: زُبَر
27.2.5.meaning: Billets of iron awaiting the smith.

28.2.3.head: جَأش
28.2.3.meaning: The heart or spirit, particularly its steadiness under strain.

30.1.2.head: حَميت
30.1.2.meaning: Pure or unadulterated in taste or colour.

32.1.5.head: أَسَف
32.1.5.meaning: Grief mixed with anger or regret.

32.2.2.meaning: To turn fierce like a leopard.

33.2.5.head: ظَفَر
33.2.5.meaning: Victory, echoing the Arabic word for a claw.

35.1.5.head: لَجَب
35.1.5.meaning: The mingled clamour of many voices.

36.2.2.head: نَبهان
36.2.2.meaning: Nabhan, a branch of Tayy from which Khutama descends.

37.1.6.head: أُدَد
37.1.6.meaning: Udad, the father of Tayy in the traditional genealogy.

39.1.4.head: غِبّ
39.1.4.meaning: Immediately after, in the wake of.

40.1.2.head: عَقائِق
40.1.2.meaning: Carnelian or agate beads, especially the reddish sort.

40.2.4-5.head: الوَشي وَالحِبَر
40.2.4-5.meaning: Figured cloth and striped or patterned robes.

41.2.1.head: أَضعاف
41.2.1.meaning: The folds or inner parts. Al-Sayrafi’s text has “kinds” in its place.
